title: One Clock

script.text: China is about five time zones wide. It runs on one clock.

script: From the Pamir Mountains to the Amur River, it spans over [60|sixty] degrees of longitude.
The sun needs about four hours to cross it.

script.text: But every clock reads Beijing Time. [UTC+8|U T C plus eight].

script: Until [1949|nineteen forty-nine], China had five time zones. Then the new government made it one.
Now watch the sun move. The clocks don't care.
Out west in Kashgar, solar noon arrives around [3 PM|three P M].
In winter, sunrise comes around [10 AM|ten A M].
In summer, sunset is after [10 PM|ten P M].

script.text: Kashgar's clock runs about [3 hours|three hours] ahead of its sun.

script: So many [Uyghurs|Wee-gurs] keep their own, unofficial clock. Xinjiang Time. Two hours behind Beijing.
And at the Afghan border, in the Wakhan Corridor, the clock jumps [3½|three and a half] hours.

script.text: The biggest clock jump across any land border on Earth.

script: One country. One clock. And the sun still keeps five.
sources: Kashgar sun times: own NOAA-style calculation at 39.47N 75.99E (Dec 1 sunrise 09:57, Jan 5 10:16, solar noon 14:45-15:01, Jun 21 sunset 22:26, all Beijing Time)
